innate-immunity.short: The fast, general first defence: skin and mucus barriers plus cells such as neutrophils and natural killer cells. It reacts the same way to every germ and has no memory.

adaptive-immunity.short: The slower, specific defence run by lymphocytes (T and B cells). It learns one germ, makes antibodies against it and remembers it, so a second meeting is faster.

leukocyte.short: White blood cell: any immune cell that travels in the blood. Neutrophils, lymphocytes and monocytes are all leukocytes.

neutrophil.short: The most common leukocyte and a first responder of innate immunity. It finds bacteria and engulfs them.

lymphocyte.short: A leukocyte of adaptive immunity (T cells and B cells), plus natural killer cells. Most sit in lymph nodes, spleen, gut and lungs; only a part is in the blood.

nk-cell.short: A lymphocyte of innate immunity that kills virus-infected or damaged cells quickly, without needing to learn the germ first.

leukocytosis.short: A rise in the number of leukocytes in the blood. In exercise it comes from cells released from vessel walls and organs, not from new cells.

lymphopenia.short: A low number of lymphocytes in the blood. After hard exercise it is brief, and cells are thought to have moved to tissues rather than died.

open-window.short: The idea that for some hours after heavy exercise the immune system is weakened, so germs can get in more easily. Its strength is debated.

salivary-iga.short: Immunoglobulin A in saliva: an antibody that guards the mouth and throat lining. It is easy to collect, so studies often use it as a sign of mucosal defence.

immune-surveillance.short: The immune system's routine patrol: cells moving through tissues and checking for germs, stressed cells and tumour cells.

immune-marker.short: A measurable sign of immune function, such as cell counts in blood, NK cell activity or salivary IgA. A marker is not the same as getting ill.

urti.short: A cold-type illness of nose, throat and upper airway: runny nose, sore throat, sneezing. Mostly caused by viruses such as rhinovirus.

incidence-rate.short: How many new cases happen among a group in a set time, often written per 1,000 athletes. Divide cases by athletes, then multiply by 1,000.

j-curve.short: A model: illness risk is lowest with moderate training, higher with none, and highest after prolonged, heavy training. Drawn, it looks like the letter J.

neck-check.short: A rule of thumb: if symptoms are only above the neck (runny nose, mild sore throat) light training may be fine; below the neck (fever, chest, body aches) rest.

myocarditis.short: Inflammation of the heart muscle, usually from a virus. Rare, but it is the main serious risk of hard exercise during a viral illness.
